# E04 — Signed implementation scope and responsibility schedule

Record version: SOW-218.2.0. Owner: Delivery Operations. Signed: 2025-01-20. Status: incorporated into executed order E02; supersedes pre-contract checklist D0.

The contracted workflow begins when Vela confirms an approved order in its sales system. RelayGrid must ingest the event, retain a durable order reference, pass a validated reservation request through the supported warehouse connector and expose a reconciled operational status. Northstar must transform Vela's item and customer codes according to the agreed field map. Vela must supply correct master data, nominated acceptance users and usable service-account access. Northstar manages the invoice adapter from warehouse shipment confirmation to Vela's accounting service. RelayGrid supplies implementation coordination, connector configuration, test support and a readiness report covering these joined components.

Appendix B divides technical ownership. RelayGrid owns connector retry behavior and duplicate suppression within its service boundary. Northstar owns transformation version control and the accounting adapter. Vela owns business meaning of item codes and account permissions. The clause on customer dependencies allows schedule adjustment for a documented unmet dependency that materially affects the critical path. It requires prompt written notice identifying impact and corrective work. It does not automatically convert every defect to a customer charge or suspend delivery work while allocation is disputed.

Acceptance requires an end-to-end demonstration of order ingest, correct reservation, shipment acknowledgment, invoice creation and reconciliation using agreed representative cases. No unresolved severity-one defect may remain. Severity-two defects need a documented workaround, business-owner acceptance and delivery approval. The representative set includes duplicate notification, delayed acknowledgment, warehouse outage and partial shipment. A successful transport response alone is not acceptance. Vela has five business days after the readiness report to sign acceptance or identify unmet criteria. That review window has not started because no final report has been delivered.

The target date is June 16, contingent on scheduled readiness work and documented dependencies. Date changes must use the change-control process with impact, owners and signatories. Support can state the present technical facts but cannot unilaterally amend the signed target or bind Atlas. A limited pilot may be separately authorized without treating incomplete full-scope work as accepted. A pilot's commercial meaning depends on the written authorization and its relation to the acceptance criteria; the label pilot alone changes no contract.

Change control distinguishes correcting a contracted defect from requesting a new feature. A request for a second regional warehouse is outside this scope. Reliable handling of repeat events for the first warehouse is within the signed boundary. A four-way ownership meeting is scheduled for June 12 at 15:00. The contract does not require an allocation verdict before safe troubleshooting, preservation or a customer risk update. # E05 — Current launch control and operational acceptance policy

Record version: DEL-4.3. Owner: RelayGrid Delivery Assurance. Effective: 2025-05-01. Case applicability annotation: 2025-06-12 12:20 UTC. Status: current internal operating policy, communicated to implementation staff May 1; project-specific references reflect the later applicability annotation.

A launch status describes a bounded configuration, workload and time. Staff must not use ready without naming what has passed, what remains open and who can authorize the switch. Production tenant availability, a successful demonstration and signed customer acceptance are separate events. The policy requires a current defect register, tested recovery procedure, customer operations owner, monitoring owner and explicit go/no-go record before primary commercial processing begins. Contract-specific acceptance terms remain applicable; an internal status cannot remove a signed deliverable.

Severity one means observed or reasonably foreseeable corruption, duplication or loss of a commercial transaction without a proven containment mechanism. It blocks unattended production processing. Severity two means a material workflow defect with a verified bounded workaround and auditable recovery. A downgrade needs Delivery Assurance approval based on test evidence, not a salesperson's preference or a quieter dashboard. Synthetic staging can proceed under a test permit if isolated from commercial events. Commercial pilots require a scoped operational exception under the current authority matrix and customer approval. An exception does not declare the full implementation complete.

A launch request must identify the event path, data snapshot, software versions, volume limits, excluded operations and rollback trigger. After a failure, staff must compare source intent, durable event receipt, downstream commit and reconciliation rather than infer business success from a transport acknowledgment. Retries may reapply a business effect if suppression is incomplete. Replaying an entire batch against live systems requires an approved reconciliation plan because an earlier apparent failure may have committed downstream. Duplicate reservations can block inventory even when no duplicate invoice is issued.

Support leads may schedule reviews, preserve case records, correct misleading customer statements and keep milestone invoicing blocked where acceptance is absent. They cannot accept business risk for the customer, waive contract criteria, authorize partner spend or guarantee another company's response. They must provide a bounded update when a requested outcome is not yet known. A missed specialist checkpoint requires a timely status update, escalation to the duty delivery director and a revised controlled commitment. Silence until a full diagnosis is available is not an approved process.

The policy provides no bonus for launching by an advertised date. Where launch incentives exist, the decision record must retain failed tests and unresolved responsibility claims. A customer may reasonably prefer a slower complete cutover or a limited usable process, but customer urgency is not consent to undisclosed risk. A customer signature procured by describing an untested workflow as reliable does not cure the underlying disclosure problem. Archived DEL-3.1 in E06 is retained because a project ticket still links to it. Its simplified project closure fields must not be used as current authority to trigger final billing or declare the implementation accepted.
# E06 — Superseded implementation playbook and inherited ticket

Record version: DEL-3.1. Owner: Delivery Operations archive. Effective: 2024-09-01 through 2025-04-30. Retrieved into project ticket: 2025-05-06. Status: superseded; retained to explain a live workflow reference.

Vela ticket IMP-218 was created February 3 from this template. Its closure checklist still contains a link to DEL-3.1 and a field named customer endpoint complete. # E08 — RelayGrid connector findings and limits

Record version: ENG-218.6. Owner: engineer Jules Tran. Dated: 2025-06-12 10:45 UTC. Status: preliminary reproducible findings from staging T-41; no commercial order replay authorized.

T-41 contained 240 synthetic order events covering 120 distinct orders. Testers intentionally repeated each initial event once after simulated acknowledgment loss. Every request reached RelayGrid's gateway, and 240 transport acknowledgments were returned. The warehouse emulator recorded 123 reservations: 117 orders had one reservation and three orders had two. No invoice was produced because the accounting adapter was disabled for this run. Successful transport delivery therefore coexists with three duplicate business effects; an all-green gateway dashboard alone is not an operational success measure.

The duplicates occur on the path where the warehouse commits a reservation but the connector loses the response. Retry key handling uses a local attempt identifier on that branch instead of the durable source order reference. RelayGrid owns this branch under Appendix B. Jules reproduced the defect with the unchanged baseline mapping. This supports a vendor defect independent of Vela's late classification file. It does not establish that all failures in earlier batches had the same cause or that Northstar's transformation never contributes to other problems. An engineer can accept responsibility for a boundary without deciding every commercial claim.

Patch C-19 changes the retry key and adds an audit record. It passed the narrow duplicate test at 09:50 with 120 distinct orders and 120 reservations. The patch is in staging only. It has not passed the warehouse outage, partial shipment, accounting reconciliation or representative-volume tests. Jules estimates one engineer-day to complete targeted tests if the warehouse sandbox remains available, with broader testing possibly longer. This is an effort estimate, not a promise of production readiness by June 16. A release candidate would still need change approval and customer operational sign-off.

There is a separate stale-status issue. When the warehouse rejects a mapped item, RelayGrid displays received until the rejection polling task runs. The task currently runs every fifteen minutes in staging. A user may read received as reserved, though the UI legend distinguishes them. Engineering can change the label and improve alerting, but neither change validates an incorrect mapping. Test operators need the source reference and downstream commit report for reconciliation. The dashboard retains failed attempts; it must not be filtered to make the launch record appear cleaner.

Production impact is limited by the current route: the legacy feed remains primary and the new connector has not been authorized to transmit live orders. Two duplicate reservations discussed by Owen belong to staging batch T-40, not known commercial shipments. Production tenant credentials exist but no evidence establishes a general live switch. Engineering has no record that Vela inventory or funds have been lost. Preservation of staging logs and versions through July 12 is requested because ownership remains disputed. Log retention does not itself authorize sharing credentials, personal customer data or unrelated tenant records with the partner.

# E10 — Vela operations constraints and business test evidence

Record version: OPS-V218.5. Owner: warehouse manager Dana Fox. Dated: 2025-06-12 11:20 UTC. Status: authenticated operational evidence; not contractual acceptance.

The primary warehouse processes an average of 180 orders daily and can reach 360 on promotion days. Atlas represents about eighty daily orders, spread across morning and afternoon releases. Dana tested seven business scenarios on June 11. Basic single-item orders and ordinary shipment confirmation worked. A mixed pack-size order reserved the wrong quantity with M8. The test form was signed attended by Dana and observed by Owen, in fields used to record participation. # E11 — Sales correspondence, readiness language and quarter forecast

Record version: CRM-218.7. Owner: account executive Alec Rowan. Compiled: 2025-06-12 10:10 UTC. Status: preserved synthetic correspondence and internal forecast; no signed scope amendment.

# E04 — Signed implementation scope and responsibility schedule

Record version: SOW-218.2.0. Owner: Delivery Operations. Signed: 2025-01-20. Status: incorporated into executed order E02; supersedes pre-contract checklist D0.

The contracted workflow begins when Vela confirms an approved order in its sales system. RelayGrid must ingest the event, retain a durable order reference, pass a validated reservation request through the supported warehouse connector and expose a reconciled operational status. Northstar must transform Vela's item and customer codes according to the agreed field map. Vela must supply correct master data, nominated acceptance users and usable service-account access. Northstar manages the invoice adapter from warehouse shipment confirmation to Vela's accounting service. RelayGrid supplies implementation coordination, connector configuration, test support and a readiness report covering these joined components.

Appendix B divides technical ownership. RelayGrid owns connector retry behavior and duplicate suppression within its service boundary. Northstar owns transformation version control and the accounting adapter. Vela owns business meaning of item codes and account permissions. The clause on customer dependencies allows schedule adjustment for a documented unmet dependency that materially affects the critical path. It requires prompt written notice identifying impact and corrective work. It does not automatically convert every defect to a customer charge or suspend delivery work while allocation is disputed.

Acceptance requires an end-to-end demonstration of order ingest, correct reservation, shipment acknowledgment, invoice creation and reconciliation using agreed representative cases. No unresolved severity-one defect may remain. Severity-two defects need a documented workaround, business-owner acceptance and delivery approval. The representative set includes duplicate notification, delayed acknowledgment, warehouse outage and partial shipment. A successful transport response alone is not acceptance. Vela has five business days after the readiness report to sign acceptance or identify unmet criteria. That review window has not started because no final report has been delivered.

The target date is June 16, contingent on scheduled readiness work and documented dependencies. Date changes must use the change-control process with impact, owners and signatories. Support can state the present technical facts but cannot unilaterally amend the signed target or bind Atlas. A limited pilot may be separately authorized without treating incomplete full-scope work as accepted. A pilot's commercial meaning depends on the written authorization and its relation to the acceptance criteria; the label pilot alone changes no contract.

Change control distinguishes correcting a contracted defect from requesting a new feature. A request for a second regional warehouse is outside this scope. Reliable handling of repeat events for the first warehouse is within the signed boundary. A four-way ownership meeting is scheduled for June 12 at 15:00. The contract does not require an allocation verdict before safe troubleshooting, preservation or a customer risk update. Northstar's commercial agreement is separate; RelayGrid cannot promise unlimited partner labor or give Northstar access beyond Vela's grant. Costs and loss claims require the approval matrix, not an informal meeting majority.
# E05 — Current launch control and operational acceptance policy

Record version: DEL-4.3. Owner: RelayGrid Delivery Assurance. Effective: 2025-05-01. Case applicability annotation: 2025-06-12 12:20 UTC. Status: current internal operating policy, communicated to implementation staff May 1; project-specific references reflect the later applicability annotation.

A launch status describes a bounded configuration, workload and time. Staff must not use ready without naming what has passed, what remains open and who can authorize the switch. Production tenant availability, a successful demonstration and signed customer acceptance are separate events. The policy requires a current defect register, tested recovery procedure, customer operations owner, monitoring owner and explicit go/no-go record before primary commercial processing begins. Contract-specific acceptance terms remain applicable; an internal status cannot remove a signed deliverable.

Severity one means observed or reasonably foreseeable corruption, duplication or loss of a commercial transaction without a proven containment mechanism. It blocks unattended production processing. Severity two means a material workflow defect with a verified bounded workaround and auditable recovery. A downgrade needs Delivery Assurance approval based on test evidence, not a salesperson's preference or a quieter dashboard. Synthetic staging can proceed under a test permit if isolated from commercial events. Commercial pilots require a scoped operational exception under the current authority matrix and customer approval. An exception does not declare the full implementation complete.

A launch request must identify the event path, data snapshot, software versions, volume limits, excluded operations and rollback trigger. After a failure, staff must compare source intent, durable event receipt, downstream commit and reconciliation rather than infer business success from a transport acknowledgment. Retries may reapply a business effect if suppression is incomplete. Replaying an entire batch against live systems requires an approved reconciliation plan because an earlier apparent failure may have committed downstream. Duplicate reservations can block inventory even when no duplicate invoice is issued.

Support leads may schedule reviews, preserve case records, correct misleading customer statements and keep milestone invoicing blocked where acceptance is absent. They cannot accept business risk for the customer, waive contract criteria, authorize partner spend or guarantee another company's response. They must provide a bounded update when a requested outcome is not yet known. A missed specialist checkpoint requires a timely status update, escalation to the duty delivery director and a revised controlled commitment. Silence until a full diagnosis is available is not an approved process.

The policy provides no bonus for launching by an advertised date. Where launch incentives exist, the decision record must retain failed tests and unresolved responsibility claims. A customer may reasonably prefer a slower complete cutover or a limited usable process, but customer urgency is not consent to undisclosed risk. A customer signature procured by describing an untested workflow as reliable does not cure the underlying disclosure problem. Archived DEL-3.1 in E06 is retained because a project ticket still links to it. Its simplified project closure fields must not be used as current authority to trigger final billing or declare the implementation accepted.
# E06 — Superseded implementation playbook and inherited ticket

Record version: DEL-3.1. Owner: Delivery Operations archive. Effective: 2024-09-01 through 2025-04-30. Retrieved into project ticket: 2025-05-06. Status: superseded; retained to explain a live workflow reference.

Vela ticket IMP-218 was created February 3 from this template. Its closure checklist still contains a link to DEL-3.1 and a field named customer endpoint complete. Alec's June 10 account forecast cites the tile as a signal that the implementation will count as delivered this quarter. Finance's acceptance gate is independent of that forecast. The old template also contains a placeholder for a premium support quote, which did not create a customer order. Neither the template nor Alec's forecast records Sera's agreement to purchase more service. A commercial report can explain staff pressure without supplying technical readiness or customer consent.

# E08 — RelayGrid connector findings and limits

Record version: ENG-218.6. Owner: engineer Jules Tran. Dated: 2025-06-12 10:45 UTC. Status: preliminary reproducible findings from staging T-41; no commercial order replay authorized.

T-41 contained 240 synthetic order events covering 120 distinct orders. Testers intentionally repeated each initial event once after simulated acknowledgment loss. Every request reached RelayGrid's gateway, and 240 transport acknowledgments were returned. The warehouse emulator recorded 123 reservations: 117 orders had one reservation and three orders had two. No invoice was produced because the accounting adapter was disabled for this run. Successful transport delivery therefore coexists with three duplicate business effects; an all-green gateway dashboard alone is not an operational success measure.

The duplicates occur on the path where the warehouse commits a reservation but the connector loses the response. Retry key handling uses a local attempt identifier on that branch instead of the durable source order reference. RelayGrid owns this branch under Appendix B. Jules reproduced the defect with the unchanged baseline mapping. This supports a vendor defect independent of Vela's late classification file. It does not establish that all failures in earlier batches had the same cause or that Northstar's transformation never contributes to other problems. An engineer can accept responsibility for a boundary without deciding every commercial claim.

Patch C-19 changes the retry key and adds an audit record. It passed the narrow duplicate test at 09:50 with 120 distinct orders and 120 reservations. The patch is in staging only. It has not passed the warehouse outage, partial shipment, accounting reconciliation or representative-volume tests. Jules estimates one engineer-day to complete targeted tests if the warehouse sandbox remains available, with broader testing possibly longer. This is an effort estimate, not a promise of production readiness by June 16. A release candidate would still need change approval and customer operational sign-off.

There is a separate stale-status issue. When the warehouse rejects a mapped item, RelayGrid displays received until the rejection polling task runs. The task currently runs every fifteen minutes in staging. A user may read received as reserved, though the UI legend distinguishes them. Engineering can change the label and improve alerting, but neither change validates an incorrect mapping. Test operators need the source reference and downstream commit report for reconciliation. The dashboard retains failed attempts; it must not be filtered to make the launch record appear cleaner.

Production impact is limited by the current route: the legacy feed remains primary and the new connector has not been authorized to transmit live orders. Two duplicate reservations discussed by Owen belong to staging batch T-40, not known commercial shipments. Production tenant credentials exist but no evidence establishes a general live switch. Engineering has no record that Vela inventory or funds have been lost. Preservation of staging logs and versions through July 12 is requested because ownership remains disputed. Log retention does not itself authorize sharing credentials, personal customer data or unrelated tenant records with the partner.

# E12 — Recovery runbook, deployment prerequisites and rollback

Record version: RUN-218.4. Owner: Delivery Assurance lead Ivo Santos. Dated: 2025-06-12 11:45 UTC. Status: proposed operational runbook; no production authorization implied.

Staging work can proceed today using C-19 and M9 in an isolated tenant. Jules owns connector deployment, Pavel owns mapping deployment and Owen confirms the business table. Each run records the source-order list, mapping version, connector version and warehouse report before the nightly reset. The sequence includes ordinary orders, repeated notification after lost response, warehouse unavailability, partial shipment and invoice reconciliation. Passing a subset is reported as a subset. The record must include rejected lines and duplicate downstream effects, not only successful gateway requests.

For a commercial pilot, Vela must select at most twenty orders per day from a single warehouse and remove those exact references from the legacy transmission list. A Vela operator checks item quantities and one warehouse reservation before approving release. Automatic retries and invoice release stay disabled. The operator reconciles source intent, warehouse commit and accounting status at least every two hours. Dana holds a stop control and Mira coordinates support. The production credential must be rotated through the restricted process before any pilot path can be enabled. These are proposed controls, not evidence that Sera has consented or that all approval signatures exist.

A confirmed duplicate reservation, unexplained quantity difference, missing event trace or inability to reconcile within two hours stops the pilot. Stop means disable new pilot intake, preserve the batch, identify already committed orders and reconcile them with Dana before further action. It does not mean replay everything through the legacy feed immediately. Some reservations may already exist. Jules estimates the route can be disabled in ten minutes, but inventory reconciliation can take longer and depends on warehouse access. No zero-loss or instant rollback guarantee is supported.

A full cutover requires more than the pilot controls. Current representative-volume testing, partial shipment invoicing, a restoration rehearsal, support staffing and signed end-to-end acceptance remain outstanding. The deployment team has not booked an unattended overnight production window. Ivo will review actual evidence at June 13 10:00 UTC and publish whether test gates passed, failed or remain incomplete. Nia's go/no-go meeting is June 13 11:00. Those meetings can decide scope or defer it; they are not appointments at which readiness is guaranteed to become true.

If Vela chooses to retain legacy processing, keep the new connector off the commercial path and continue corrective staging work. The legacy extension needs procurement action before June 13 noon, and the retailer waiver has its own 16:00 notice deadline. RelayGrid cannot resolve those dependencies by unilaterally updating its project target. If a supplier or customer approver misses a checkpoint, Mira reports the actual state by the next committed update and escalates to Nia. An exception may be considered only from evidence of a bounded workload and explicit authority; a project label or favorable customer sentiment is not a substitute for these controls.
# E13 — Customer communication and launch claims guidance

Record version: COM-6.2. Owner: RelayGrid Communications. Effective: 2025-05-15. Status: current general brand guidance for delivery escalations.

Customer language should connect the observed failure to the customer's practical decision. Acknowledge the impact of unreliable operations and explain what the vendor owns. Do not make the customer translate internal queue names or mediate a dispute between teams before receiving help. One support owner can coordinate work without pretending to control every supplier. Naming technical dependencies is useful when it explains a limit or needed action; listing every organization to diffuse responsibility is not. The external reply should make the next owner and update time easy to find.

Do not describe a production tenant as a completed implementation unless the relevant workflow and acceptance states support it. When earlier language created an incorrect impression, correct it directly. An apology need not concede every legal claim, and avoidance of an absolute liability conclusion need not make the reply evasive. Distinguish responsibility for a reproduced connector defect from allocation of all project delay. Facts can be acknowledged before an exhaustive root-cause or damages review. Customer allegations should be attributed fairly rather than repeated as proven technical findings.

Use ordinary operational terms. Received means the gateway accepted a message; reserved means the warehouse recorded inventory; invoiced means the accounting service created a document. If those distinctions matter to the proposed course, explain them briefly. Do not overwhelm the board briefing with implementation jargon or paste raw logs. A limited workload must be described as limited. Pilot controls should not be represented as proof the agreed full workflow is ready. Words such as guaranteed, fully resolved and seamless require evidence and appropriate authority.

Sales support may assist in resolving a customer problem, but basic delivery correction must not be sold again under an emergency premium plan. Optional service may be described accurately when its actual limits are relevant, with the customer free to decline. A quote expiry must not be presented as a condition for honoring an existing contract or a previously approved reimbursement. Do not request positive publicity, silence, a reference call or an acceptance certificate in exchange for corrective work. The customer's public criticism does not change technical truth or financial authority.

Every written update should distinguish decisions taken, actions proposed and matters awaiting approval. An update deadline is a commitment the support team can control; a repair completion time may depend on unverified tests. If no new result arrives, the owner still explains the current state, what blocked progress and the next decision time. Brand review does not require hiding failures to protect a launch narrative. This policy does not prescribe which operational route Vela should choose; it governs the honesty and usefulness of the communication supporting that choice. Specific confidential partner pricing and personal data remain subject to the disclosure controls, even when transparency is appropriate.
# E14 — Support ownership, staffed windows and escalation commitments

Record version: SUP-218.5. Owner: support manager Mira Chen. Dated: 2025-06-12 12:30 UTC. Status: confirmed service coordination schedule; does not certify readiness.

Mira owns the customer response through June 13 at 18:00 UTC and is responsible for the promised June 12 16:30 update. She will chair today's 15:00 integration session and maintain one shared dependency register. Jules is the RelayGrid engineering owner for the retry defect and test evidence. Ivo owns operational risk review. Nia decides delivery exceptions and financial use of R-218. Pavel owns Northstar's transformation report within his confirmed session. Owen owns Vela's business mapping and access coordination. Dana owns customer-side reconciliation and can stop unsafe warehouse testing. Sera retains business and contractual choice.

Today's integration session runs 15:00 to 17:00. Its first thirty minutes will compare the failing reproduction, map M9 and agreed acceptance criteria. By 16:00 each owner must identify a current next action, prerequisite and expected evidence time. Mira's 16:30 written update need not await the full session. If tests are still running, she can report that state, preserve the legacy primary route and identify the June 13 checkpoint. If an owner is absent, she escalates that dependency to Nia immediately rather than assign work to an unconsenting team.

Jules is staffed until 18:00 today and from 08:00 to 18:00 June 13. RelayGrid has a duty engineer over the weekend for operational emergencies; that roster is not a full implementation squad and cannot be promised as one. Nia can approve additional RelayGrid staffing within the sixty-hour allocation after checking availability. Northstar's weekend engineers are not confirmed. Vela's two trained operators can cover Friday; Saturday's one operator is a capacity constraint. These limits must be reflected in any pilot proposal instead of assuming that an escalation magically supplies unlimited resources.

Finance Operations contact Amira Lane can keep milestone M3-218 blocked immediately on Mira's request. Once a reimbursement is chosen and substantiated, Amira verifies the invoice and checks recipient company details through the established account channel. Normal submission is next business day after a complete request. A reimbursement submitted Friday may reach the customer later; support must distinguish submission, approval and bank receipt. M3 remains unissued regardless of whether Vela chooses a pilot or legacy extension, unless actual full-scope acceptance is later recorded.

If today's update is missed, Mira's deputy Ren Ortiz must notify Sera before 17:00, explain the missed commitment and state who now owns the next update. The handoff must include real route state, tests, approvals, pending consent and upcoming external deadlines.
